panel.title: Overhead and underground power lines: what the law says
panel.intro: The legal regime for high- and medium-voltage lines combines three national laws. Ley 24/2013, of 26 December, on the Electricity Sector (BOE-A-2013-13645) sets the framework for planning, authorisation, expropriation and rights of way for transport and distribution installations, and requires them to be coordinated with urban planning. Royal Decree 223/2008 (BOE-A-2008-5269) approves the High-Voltage Lines Regulation and its nine complementary technical instructions (ITC-LAT 01 to 09), which set the technical and safety conditions for each type of line. And Royal Decree 1955/2000 (art. 112) requires the planning of these installations to be coordinated with the relevant urban or territorial planning instruments, reserving land for both new lines and the protection of existing ones.
panel.overhead: Overhead lines — such as the three high-voltage lines that cross the north of the neighbourhood through the El Manchón area, plus two medium-voltage lines with supports on Calle Tilo (municipal question, Feb. 2022) — are technically governed by ITC-LAT 07 (bare conductors) or ITC-LAT 08 (insulated cables) under RD 223/2008, which set their safety clearances. Under planning law, article 6.6.28 of Seville's General Urban Plan (PGOU) allows overhead lines on urban land as a basic-infrastructure use of general interest, but on consolidated urban land it requires technical justification for not burying the line. That is why the lines currently flying over the houses of La Bachillera are treated as an unresolved situation, not as the ordinary regime intended for an already-consolidated neighbourhood.
panel.underground: Underground lines are governed by ITC-LAT 06 (underground lines with insulated cables) under RD 223/2008, which regulates their depth, protection and crossings. It is also the regime Seville's PGOU favours: on non-consolidated urban land and on land designated for development, article 6.6.28 (sections 5, 6 and 11) requires new lines built as part of a development to be buried, and on consolidated urban land underground routing is the default option, only replaceable by an overhead line if it is technically justified as unfeasible.
panel.bachilleraCase: The specific case for the neighbourhood is Modificación Puntual nº 67 of Seville's PGOU, in process in 2026, covering the area around the «Empalme» substation (San Jerónimo). It reverses the 2006 plan, which envisaged relocating the substation to free up land for housing, and instead opts to secure it on its current site as critical infrastructure for the provincial power grid. The chosen option — «Alternativa Tres» — routes the new streets around the substation's perimeter without expropriating any homes in La Bachillera, and includes rerouting and burying the overhead lines that currently fly over the neighbourhood, a resident demand that municipal groups had already raised in 2022 (question to the mayor, Apr. 2022). No official document for this amendment has been located on the Gerencia de Urbanismo's website or in the Seville provincial bulletin (BOP); this paragraph is based on a press source (report, July 2026) and should be treated as unconfirmed until it is published officially.

popup.overheadNote: Overhead high- or medium-voltage line section (ITC-LAT 07 or 08, RD 223/2008). On consolidated urban land, Seville's PGOU requires justification for why it has not been buried.
popup.undergroundNote: Underground line section with insulated cables (ITC-LAT 06, RD 223/2008). Seville's PGOU requires this routing in new developments and also favours it on consolidated urban land.

home.legalParagraph: The high- and medium-voltage lines crossing La Bachillera — through El Manchón and through the centre of the neighbourhood — are legally compatible with urban land, but the PGOU favours burying them on consolidated urban land (art. 6.6.28), and municipal groups have been demanding a timeline for that since 2022. Modificación Puntual nº 67, now in process, proposes rerouting and burying these lines alongside securing the «Empalme» substation.

methodology.linesBody: The power-line layer comes from © OpenStreetMap contributors, under the Open Database License (ODbL), extracted on {{date}}. OpenStreetMap does distinguish overhead from underground routing, but underground lines are clearly under-mapped: many buried sections — especially in recent developments — have not yet been digitised, so a missing line on the map is no guarantee that no buried line exists there. By contrast, the official DERA layer from IDEAndalucía (Instituto de Estadística y Cartografía de Andalucía, CC BY 4.0 licence) geolocates Andalusia's power lines, but its data does not distinguish whether a section is overhead or underground, so it cannot replace OSM for that distinction and is used here only as contextual reference.
